tldr: Even across humanoids with different joint-axis layouts, aligning reinforcement learning policy outputs and observations to shared, body-aligned virtual joints with an analytical coordinate transform allows the exact same training recipe to be reused without retuning any rewards or hyperparameters.

In contrast, the bottom row's proposed method unifies them into a shared body-aligned virtual joint space (roll, pitch, yaw), giving identical motion commands the exact same geometric meaning.
overview:
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled dynamic humanoid locomotion. However, whenever a different robot is introduced, training recipes—reward functions, hyperparameters, and architectures—must be manually retuned from scratch.

This happens because many humanoids mount their rotational axes, such as in the hips, at oblique angles to save packaging space for actuators and expand their range of motion. Typically, an RL policy directly outputs native joint angles specific to the robot. On a robot with oblique axes, even a simple movement like swinging a leg forward requires delicately coordinating multiple joints. As a result, how exploration is normalized and how regularization penalties affect learning drastically shift from robot to robot.

To solve this, the authors propose inserting a body-aligned virtual joint space at the policy's input and output layers. The policy is trained on shared, anatomically natural virtual joints. Just before passing targets to existing transmissions and low-level controllers, a forward-kinematics-based deterministic layer analytically maps these virtual targets into native joint angles. Furthermore, by training on an idealized orthogonal-axis model and inserting the mapping layer only at deployment (a "post-hoc" mapping approach), optimization instability during training is completely avoided.

In simulation across three humanoids with vastly different joint layouts, using a single unmodified recipe, this method was the only one where foot orientation remained aligned with the travel direction while walking stably across all three robots. In straight-line walking tests on the physical Unitree G1 robot, it reduced heading drift by nearly a factor of six compared to the conventional native coordinate interface.
contributions: Pinpointed that the main obstacle preventing training recipe reuse across robots is not the actuator transmission mechanism, but the geometric mismatch of native joint coordinate systems directly exposed to the policy

Formulated an analytical, forward-kinematics-based deterministic coordinate transformation layer that converts between a shared body-aligned orthogonal coordinate frame (virtual joints) and each robot's native joint space

Demonstrated that training instability can be drastically suppressed by training the policy on an orthogonal model and applying the virtual joint mapping post-hoc, rather than embedding the mapping inside the training loop
Achieved natural, stable locomotion with minimal drift across three humanoids with different leg-axis layouts and on physical Unitree G1 hardware, without changing a single recipe parameter

sections.heading: Why Can't Humanoid Locomotion Training Recipes Be Reused?
sections.summary: RL-based locomotion control has shown remarkable results, but training setups cannot be carried over when switching to a new robot. This is caused by obliquely tilted joint axes resulting from mechanical packaging, combined with policies commanding actions directly in native joint space.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated high locomotion performance on both quadrupeds and bipeds, including zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. However, whenever a new robot appears, engineers must spend enormous amounts of time retuning reward weights and hyperparameters.

At the root of this issue lie hardware design differences across robots. To reduce distal mass and inertia while generating high torque within tight spaces, humanoid legs often place actuators away from joint centers, use linkage mechanisms, or tilt joint rotation axes at oblique angles. Consequently, rotational axes are not orthogonal to the body; instead, they form complex, oblique, and coupled configurations.

The real problem is that standard locomotion policies directly output robot-specific native joint angles. For example, consider opening a leg straight to the side relative to the body (hip roll). If the joint axes are orthogonal, moving a single joint is enough. But on a robot with oblique axes, multiple joints must be coordinated simultaneously. This means that for the exact same walking task, the numerical representation the policy needs to learn differs completely between robots.

Furthermore, practical RL typically samples exploration via diagonal Gaussian distributions per joint, and defines action scales, PD gains, and regularization penalties per joint. Because these are not invariant under coordinate transformations, merely tilting the joint axes severely distorts both the learning difficulty and the nature of the learned solution. Focusing on this point, the authors set out to enable the reuse of a single training recipe across different robots by introducing shared, body-aligned virtual joints upstream of robot-specific transmissions (such as four-bar linkages or parallel mechanisms).

In contrast, the proposed method in the bottom row maps them to a shared body-aligned orthogonal frame, providing a unified control interface.

sections.heading: Structural Pitfalls of Native Joint Interfaces
sections.summary: Because conventional locomotion RL defines actions and observations in native joint space, robots with oblique axes experience a breakdown between joint commands and physical link motions. This mismatch rarely shows up in coarse task metrics, leading to unnatural gaits and endless reward tweaking.
sections.details:
In humanoid reinforcement learning, the most standard approach is for the policy to output desired native joint angles $\mathbf{q}$, which are then converted into motor commands via PD controllers or an actuator transmission map $\Psi$.

### How Coordinate Differences Hurt Learning
The issue here is that even when robot $r$ and robot $s$ share the same degrees of freedom, their rotational axis directions and orderings differ. An incremental joint displacement $\Delta\mathbf{q}$ results in a link motion $\Delta\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{q}, \Delta\mathbf{q})$ that is distinct on each robot. Therefore, a policy operating in native joint space cannot just learn the locomotion task itself; it must also implicitly learn the robot's idiosyncratic coordinate geometry—namely, how to coordinate oblique axes to move the leg as intended.

### The Trap of Aggregate Metrics and Endless Tuning
Frustratingly, this geometric distortion does not readily show up in aggregate scalar metrics like tracking error for target linear velocity. Even when trained with the exact same reward function and achieving the target speed, robots may display unnatural gaits, such as walking with feet pointed outward (toe-out) or stepping with severe left-right asymmetry. Engineers are left with no choice but to visually inspect the behavior in simulation and on hardware and add robot-specific penalty rewards. This completely ruins the reusability of training recipes.

sections.heading: Designing and Integrating the Body-Aligned Virtual Joint Interface
sections.summary: Shared virtual joints aligned with the body frame are defined and mapped to native joints through a forward-kinematics-based deterministic layer. The policy trains on an idealized orthogonal model and applies the transformation at deployment (post-hoc mapping), ensuring optimization stability.
sections.details:
At the core of the proposed method is a body-aligned virtual joint interface placed at the policy's input and output layers. Instead of adding artificial joint constraints inside the physics simulation, it is computed as a kinematically deterministic layer. As a result, it leaves the robot's native dynamics and low-level control stack entirely untouched.

### Defining a Shared Body-Referenced Leg Layout
Taking the robot's body frame $\mathcal{F}_{B}$ ($x$ forward, $y$ left, $z$ up) as the reference, the humanoid leg is formulated in a standard 3-1-2 configuration (3-DoF hip, 1-DoF knee, 2-DoF ankle). The hip follows a yaw ($z$-axis), roll ($x$-axis), pitch ($y$-axis) sequence; the ankle uses roll and pitch; and the knee defines flexion as positive.

### Constructing Virtual Frames and Transforms via Link Orientations
For multi-DoF groups like the hip and ankle, relative orientations between parent links (pelvis or shin) and child links (thigh or foot) are computed via forward kinematics. Virtual angles are extracted from the relative rotation matrix $\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ after subtracting the nominal standing offset. Desired native joint angles $\Phi_r(\mathbf{q}^{V,\mathrm{des}})$ are then analytically solved via orientation matching against target virtual angles.

### Converting Velocity Observations and Gains via Jacobians
The mapping between virtual joint velocities and native joint velocities is handled bidirectionally using coordinate Jacobians $\mathbf{J}_{r}$. In addition to passing velocity observations to the policy, this also allows virtual stiffness defined in the shared virtual space (the PD controller's P-gain $\mathbf{K}^V$) to be automatically projected into native space gains as $\mathbf{K}_r = \mathbf{J}_{r}^{T} \mathbf{K}^{V} \mathbf{J}_{r}$.

### Key Architectural Choice: Post-Hoc Mapping
The authors discovered that where this mapping is placed in the system decisively impacts training stability. In an "in-loop" configuration, where the transform is evaluated at every step inside the training loop, non-linearities of the oblique axes and Jacobian singularities distort policy gradients, causing severe training instability. Instead, the proposed method trains the policy on an idealized model where joint axes are orthogonal by construction, and applies the transformation layer only during evaluation or physical deployment (a "post-hoc" format). Minor discrepancies between the idealized model and native dynamics are robustly handled as small external disturbances, keeping training remarkably stable.

sections.heading: Simulation Comparisons Across Three Distinct Robots and Hardware Validation
sections.summary: Using a single unmodified Unitree G1 recipe across three humanoids with different leg-axis layouts, only the proposed method preserved proper foot alignment and trained stably on all three. On physical G1 hardware, heading drift during straight walking dropped by nearly 6x.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
Evaluations used three humanoids with substantially different hip axis configurations: Unitree G1, PND Adam, and a custom in-house robot. The training recipe was taken directly from the official Unitree RL Lab (Isaac Lab-based) velocity tracking setup for G1. Apart from fixing the arms and waist to evaluate 12 leg DoFs, all reward weights and PPO hyperparameters were kept identical without any retuning.
Four configurations were compared: (i) native joint space, (ii) task space (controlling foot positions), (iii) virtual joints (in-loop), and (iv) the proposed virtual joints (post-hoc mapping). Simulation evaluation was conducted via Sim-to-Sim transfer into MuJoCo, which features a different contact model than the training environment.

### Tracking Performance and Foot-Progression Angle (FPA)
Across 25 evaluation velocity commands, the proposed method achieved the lowest velocity errors and least lateral drift on Adam and the custom robot, both of which feature obliquely mounted hips. Gait geometry was especially telling: evaluating the foot-progression angle (FPA) relative to the travel direction, the proposed method kept feet pointed cleanly forward with $|\mathrm{FPA}| \leq 1.3^\circ$ across all three robots. In contrast, on Adam, whose hip pitch axis is tilted by $35^\circ$, native coordinates produced a $4.8^\circ$ toe-out gait, while task space showed an extreme toe-out of $14.2^\circ$.

### Training Stability and Ablation
Measuring the proportion of unstable episodes where episode lengths suddenly collapse mid-training, the proposed post-hoc method demonstrated outstanding stability, staying below $0.1\%$ across all robots. Conversely, the in-loop variant spent $15.3\%$ of training in an unstable state on Adam, and task-space baselines were unstable for $1.2\sim 6.0\%$ of the time. This clearly validates the effectiveness of the post-hoc design.

### Physical Unitree G1 Hardware Results
Policies were deployed without any retuning onto the physical Unitree G1 robot, which had shown the smallest simulation tracking differences among coordinate frames (having only an oblique tilt of roughly $10^\circ$). Both native and in-loop policies accumulated yaw drift while walking, deviating toward the arena perimeter and forcing manual stops at $5.1\,\mathrm{m}$ and $6.9\,\mathrm{m}$, respectively. The proposed method walked the full $13.8\,\mathrm{m}$ length of the test course in a straight line. Steady-state IMU yaw rate was reduced nearly sixfold, from $5.31^\circ/\mathrm{s}$ with native control down to $0.89^\circ/\mathrm{s}$. The computational overhead on the Jetson Orin NX was minimal at roughly $0.2\,\mathrm{ms}$ (only $1\%$ of the $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ control cycle).

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Directions
sections.summary: Inserting body-aligned virtual joints bridges the geometric gap across robots with differing joint axes, allowing a single RL recipe to be reused. Future work looks toward whole-body control and motion retargeting.
sections.details:
This paper identified the native joint coordinate mismatch as the primary reason humanoid RL recipes fail to transfer across platforms, and resolved it using a body-aligned virtual joint interface.

The core strength of this method is that it acts as a purely deterministic geometric layer without modifying existing actuator transmissions or low-level PD controllers. Furthermore, real-world experiments showed that it resolves gait quality issues—such as misaligned foot progression and cumulative straight-line heading drift that do not appear in coarse simulation tracking metrics—without requiring tedious reward retuning.

Current limitations include focusing solely on 12-DoF leg velocity tracking and evaluating physical hardware on only one robot model. Moving forward, the authors plan to extend this interface to the entire body, including arms and waist, as well as apply it to motion imitation and retargeting from humans and other robots.

takeaways: Simply aligning an RL policy's action and observation spaces to body-aligned virtual joints instead of robot-specific native axes drastically improves training recipe reusability.
Embedding coordinate transforms inside the training loop causes optimization instability; training on an orthogonal model and applying the mapping post-hoc at deployment is far more robust.
Even when scalar metrics like velocity tracking error match in simulation, gait distortions from misaligned joint axes manifest as severe cumulative heading drift on real hardware.
Before hacking together robot-specific penalty rewards to fix unnatural toe-in or toe-out foot orientations, check the geometry of the policy's input/output coordinate frames.
limitations: Evaluations are limited to flat-ground velocity tracking on 12-DoF legs; effectiveness on whole-body coordination with the upper body and rough-terrain locomotion remains untested.
Hardware validation was conducted on only one platform (Unitree G1); physical testing on robots with larger axis inclinations, such as Adam, remains for future work.
Each experiment was evaluated over a limited sample of $n=3$ seeds, leaving room for broader statistical verification.
